claims.claim: Origen of Alexandria was an early Christian theologian and biblical scholar, born c. 185 and died c. 253–255.
Origen was head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria and later founded the Christian School of Caesarea.
Origen's Commentary on the Song of Songs is widely regarded as the first great work of Christian mysticism.
The Homilies on the Song of Songs seem to have been written only a few years after the Commentary, probably before 244.

Origen interpreted the Song of Songs as representing three sciences: moral science in Proverbs, natural science in Ecclesiastes, and inspective (contemplative) science in the Song of Songs, which instills love of divine and heavenly things through the figure of the Bride and Bridegroom.

Origen portrayed the Song of Songs as the unique Scripture in which the eschatological nuptials of Christ and his Bride are really present as text, and as the spirit of Scripture unveiled in all its erotic power to make the reader 'one spirit' with the Lord.
The Prologue to the Homilies is addressed to Pope Damasus, translated by St. Jerome.
Origen's spiritual reading of the Song was rooted in hermeneutical demands rather than psychological or ascetical compulsions.
